title: Task scheduler / job queue
scopeHtml:
Scope: priority and delayed jobs, worker threads with wait/notify, DelayQueue alternative.

Scope: priority and delayed jobs, worker threads with wait/notify, DelayQueue alternative.

notes.title: Requirements
notes.html:
Design an in-process task scheduler / job queue: submit jobs to run at a given time with a priority, and a pool of worker threads executes them in the right order.

Clarify:

  • Functional: submit(job) with run time and priority, N workers, shutdown.
  • Rules: earliest run time first; ties broken by higher priority; a failing job must not kill its worker.
  • Out of scope: persistence, retries with backoff, cron expressions, distributed workers (follow-ups).
  • Scale talk: Java's own ScheduledThreadPoolExecutor, Quartz, Celery, Sidekiq and AWS SQS do this at different scales; the LLD question is how workers sleep until the earliest job is due.

Worked example. At t=0 submit "late" (t+300ms), "soon" (t+100ms), "boom" (t+200ms, throws). Order of execution: soon, boom (fails, logged), late. Workers never poll in a busy loop; they wait exactly until head.runAt.

Industry examples. Sidekiq and Celery keep jobs in Redis/RabbitMQ; Kafka consumer groups are the queue-plus-workers pattern at scale; Quartz persists triggers in a database. Netflix and Uber run delayed-job systems for retries.

Everyday analogy. A kitchen ticket rail: cooks always take the ticket due soonest, and when nothing is due they wait instead of staring at the rail.

Common interview traps.

  • Busy-waiting (while(true) checking the clock) burning a CPU core.
  • Letting one exception kill a worker thread.

notes.title: Core entities
notes.html:
• Job: id, runAt (epoch ms), priority, Runnable; implements Comparable.
  • Scheduler: a PriorityQueue<Job>, a lock, and worker threads.
  • Workers: loop of wait, take, run.

Decision gravity. A heap gives O(log n) insert and O(1) peek, matching exactly "what is due next". Alternative: sorted list (O(n) insert) or a timing wheel (O(1) for huge numbers of timers, used by Netty and Kafka's delayed operations). Reversible: yes, swap the queue behind the same interface.

Everyday analogy. An alarm clock that always rings for the nearest alarm first.

Common interview traps.

  • Comparing priority before time (a high-priority far-future job would block now-due ones).
  • A compareTo that is not consistent (same job reported both less and greater).

notes.title: Class diagram
notes.html:
+----------------------+       +--------------------+
| Scheduler            | holds | Job                |
| queue: PriorityQueue |------>| id runAt priority  |
| lock, workers[]      |   *   | work: Runnable     |
| submit(Job)          |       | compareTo(): time, |
| shutdown()           |       |   then priority    |
+----------------------+       +--------------------+
        | starts
        v
   Worker thread: loop() { wait until head due; poll; run }

Common interview traps.

  • Hiding where the lock is; interviewers will ask what it protects.

notes.title: Key patterns
notes.html:
• Producer-consumer with a monitor (wait/notifyAll) so workers sleep until needed.
  • Command: a Job wraps a Runnable; the scheduler does not know what it does.
  • Template for ordering: Comparable defines the policy in one place. A Comparator passed to the queue lets you swap it (FIFO, priority, fair share).
  • Alternative using the JDK: DelayQueue plus an ExecutorService, or ScheduledThreadPoolExecutor. In real code prefer those; in an interview implement the loop to show you understand it.

Worked example. Head due in 120 ms: lock.wait(120). A new job due in 10 ms arrives: submit calls notifyAll, workers wake, re-peek, and now wait only 10 ms. Without the notify, the urgent job would sit for 110 extra ms.

Industry examples. Java's DelayQueue does exactly this with a leader/follower trick to avoid waking all threads; Netty's HashedWheelTimer and Linux timers use wheels.

Everyday analogy. A doorbell: you sleep, but a new arrival wakes you to re-plan.

Common interview traps.

  • Using if instead of while around wait (spurious wakeups).
  • Running the job while holding the lock (serialises all workers).

notes.title: Code
notes.html:
import java.util.*;
import java.util.concurrent.*;

class Job implements Comparable<Job> {
    final String id; final long runAt; final int priority; final Runnable work;
    Job(String id, long runAt, int priority, Runnable w) { this.id = id; this.runAt = runAt; this.priority = priority; work = w; }
    public int compareTo(Job o) {                       // earlier time first, then higher priority
        int c = Long.compare(runAt, o.runAt);
        return c != 0 ? c : Integer.compare(o.priority, priority);
    }
}

class Scheduler {
    private final PriorityQueue<Job> queue = new PriorityQueue<>();
    private final Object lock = new Object();
    private final Thread[] workers;
    private boolean stopped;

    Scheduler(int n) {
        workers = new Thread[n];
        for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) { workers[i] = new Thread(this::loop, "w" + i); workers[i].start(); }
    }
    void submit(Job j) { synchronized (lock) { queue.add(j); lock.notifyAll(); } }

    private void loop() {
        while (true) {
            Job j;
            synchronized (lock) {
                while (true) {
                    if (stopped) return;
                    Job head = queue.peek();
                    if (head == null) { try { lock.wait(); } catch (InterruptedException e) { return; } continue; }
                    long wait = head.runAt - System.currentTimeMillis();
                    if (wait <= 0) { j = queue.poll(); break; }
                    try { lock.wait(wait); } catch (InterruptedException e) { return; }
                }
            }
            try { j.work.run(); } catch (RuntimeException e) { System.out.println(j.id + " failed: " + e.getMessage()); }
        }
    }
    void shutdown() throws InterruptedException {
        synchronized (lock) { stopped = true; lock.notifyAll(); }
        for (Thread t : workers) t.join();
    }
}

public class Main {
    public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception {
        Scheduler s = new Scheduler(2);
        long now = System.currentTimeMillis();
        CountDownLatch done = new CountDownLatch(3);
        List<String> order = Collections.synchronizedList(new ArrayList<>());
        s.submit(new Job("late", now + 300, 1, () -> { order.add("late"); done.countDown(); }));
        s.submit(new Job("soon", now + 100, 1, () -> { order.add("soon"); done.countDown(); }));
        s.submit(new Job("boom", now + 200, 1, () -> { done.countDown(); throw new RuntimeException("bad"); }));
        done.await();
        s.shutdown();
        System.out.println(order);
        if (!order.equals(List.of("soon", "late"))) throw new AssertionError();
    }
}

Kotlin core:

class Job(val id: String, val runAt: Long, val priority: Int, val work: () -> Unit) : Comparable<Job> {
    override fun compareTo(other: Job): Int =
        compareValuesBy(this, other, { it.runAt }, { -it.priority })
}

class Scheduler(workers: Int) {
    private val queue = java.util.PriorityQueue<Job>()
    private val lock = Object()
    @Volatile private var stopped = false
    private val threads = List(workers) { Thread { loop() }.also { it.start() } }

    fun submit(j: Job) = synchronized(lock) { queue.add(j); lock.notifyAll() }

    private fun next(): Job? = synchronized(lock) {          // null means stopped
        while (!stopped) {
            val head = queue.peek()
            if (head == null) { lock.wait(); continue }
            val wait = head.runAt - System.currentTimeMillis()
            if (wait <= 0) return@synchronized queue.poll()
            lock.wait(wait)
        }
        null
    }

    private fun loop() {
        while (true) {
            val job = next() ?: return
            try { job.work() } catch (e: RuntimeException) { println("${job.id} failed: ${e.message}") }
        }
    }
    fun shutdown() { synchronized(lock) { stopped = true; lock.notifyAll() }; threads.forEach { it.join() } }
}

Common interview traps.

  • Swallowing InterruptedException without restoring the flag or exiting.

notes.title: Run and test
notes.html:
javac -d out Main.java
java -cp out Main
boom failed: bad
[soon, late]

Test: ordering with equal times (priority decides), a job submitted while workers sleep, a throwing job, shutdown while idle, many producers submitting concurrently (all jobs run exactly once).

Common interview traps.

  • Timing assertions that are flaky; assert order, not exact milliseconds.

notes.title: Concurrency
notes.html:
The code above is already the thread-safe version: one lock protects the queue and the stopped flag; workers wait on it. Key points to explain:

  1. Invariant: queue and stopped are touched only inside synchronized (lock).
  2. Lost-wakeup safety: submit adds and notifies under the same lock, and workers check the queue under the lock before waiting.
  3. No lock during execution: the job runs after the synchronized block, so N workers run N jobs in parallel.
  4. Shutdown: set flag, notifyAll, join. Jobs already running finish; queued ones are dropped (decide and say so; the alternative is draining).

Alternative using the JDK for production:

class Job implements Delayed {
    public long getDelay(TimeUnit u) { return u.convert(runAt - System.currentTimeMillis(), TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS); }
    public int compareTo(Delayed o) { return Long.compare(runAt, ((Job) o).runAt); }
}
DelayQueue<Job> q = new DelayQueue<>();
// workers: q.take().work.run();   take() blocks until the head's delay has expired

Production note (gravity). Single JVM means jobs vanish on crash. Persisting jobs in Postgres/Redis and claiming them with SELECT ... FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED lets many workers on many servers share one queue safely; this is a common, battle-tested pattern.

Common interview traps.

  • Using notify() instead of notifyAll() when workers wait for different conditions.
  • Unbounded queue with no back-pressure; say how you would bound it.

notes.title: Follow-ups
notes.html:
• Retries with exponential backoff: on failure, resubmit with runAt = now + 2^n * base.
  • Recurring jobs: after running, reschedule runAt + period.
  • Cancel a job: lazy cancellation flag checked at run time.
  • Dependencies between jobs (DAG): count of unmet parents.
  • Persistence and multiple machines: DB queue with SKIP LOCKED, or a broker.

Common interview traps.

  • Implementing retry by sleeping inside the worker, which blocks that worker.

notes.title: Summary
notes.html:
• Min-heap ordered by time then priority; workers sleep with wait(timeout) until the head is due.
  • submit must notifyAll so an earlier job re-plans the sleep.
  • One lock around the queue; run jobs outside it; catch exceptions per job.
  • DelayQueue or ScheduledThreadPoolExecutor are the production answer in a single JVM.
  • Multi-machine needs a durable queue and SKIP LOCKED or a broker.

questions.promptHtml: How do worker threads in a scheduler wait for the next job to become due, and why not loop checking the clock?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: The core mechanical idea of the problem; separates people who know monitors from those who poll.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Workers take the lock, peek the head of the priority queue and compute head.runAt - now. If the queue is empty they wait(); if the head is not due they wait(delay); if due they poll it and run it outside the lock. submit adds under the same lock and calls notifyAll, so a newly submitted earlier job wakes sleepers to re-plan. A while(true) clock check burns a whole CPU core for nothing.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
lock -> peek head
   none          -> wait()
   due in 120ms  -> wait(120)      <- a new job due in 10ms arrives: notifyAll
   due now       -> poll, unlock, RUN

Always wait in a while loop (re-check the condition after waking) because of spurious wakeups and because another worker may have taken the job. wait releases the monitor, so producers can submit while workers sleep.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
Languages: Java, Kotlin

Languages: Java · Kotlin
long wait = head.runAt - System.currentTimeMillis();
if (wait <= 0) { j = queue.poll(); break; }
lock.wait(wait);
val wait = head.runAt - System.currentTimeMillis()
if (wait <= 0) return queue.poll()
lock.wait(wait)

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• if instead of while around wait.
  • Thread.sleep inside the loop (cannot be woken by an earlier job).
  • Running the job while holding the lock.
  • Wall clock jumps: for real use prefer System.nanoTime for delays.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. What if submit forgets notifyAll? -> An urgent job waits until the current timeout ends.
  2. Why notifyAll over notify? -> Workers may wait for different conditions and a single notify could wake the wrong one.
  3. What does DelayQueue do differently? -> Leader/follower: only one thread times its wait on the head while others wait indefinitely.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE says "wait and notify". Senior says the lost-wakeup rule (add and notify under the same lock), spurious wakeups, and the leader-follower optimisation.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A cron-like service polling every 10 ms used about 12% of a core per instance across 300 instances before it was moved to timed waits.

questions.promptHtml: Why a priority queue (heap) for scheduled jobs, how should compareTo be defined, and what are the alternatives?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Tests structure choice with complexity numbers and the classic compare-order trap.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: The question the scheduler asks is "what is due next?": a min-heap gives O(log n) insert and O(1) peek. Order by runAt first, then by priority (higher first) for ties. If I compared priority first, a high-priority job set for tomorrow would sit ahead of jobs due now and block them. Alternatives: a sorted list (O(n) insert), DelayQueue, or a timing wheel for millions of timers.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
structure        insert     next due   best for
sorted list      O(n)       O(1)       tiny n
binary heap      O(log n)   O(1)       general
timing wheel     O(1)       O(1)*      millions of timers, coarse resolution

compareTo must be a consistent total order. To break ties among same time and same priority add a sequence number, otherwise FIFO among equals is not guaranteed (PriorityQueue is not stable).

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
Languages: Java, Kotlin

Languages: Java · Kotlin
public int compareTo(Job o) {
    int c = Long.compare(runAt, o.runAt);
    return c != 0 ? c : Integer.compare(o.priority, priority);
}
override fun compareTo(other: Job) =
    compareValuesBy(this, other, { it.runAt }, { -it.priority })

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Priority before time.
  • a.priority - b.priority overflow; use Integer.compare.
  • Mutating runAt of a job already in the heap (breaks the heap invariant).

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Same time and priority, who runs first? -> Undefined with a plain heap; add an insertion sequence.
  2. Cancel a job? -> Lazy flag checked at run; removing from a heap is O(n).
  3. Why do Netty and Kafka use timing wheels? -> O(1) insert for huge numbers of timeouts at coarse granularity.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE says "PriorityQueue". Senior gives complexities, the tie-break rule, and when a wheel wins.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A "priority first" comparator starved on-time jobs behind one far-future urgent job until the order was fixed.

questions.contextHtml:
A candidate's scheduler passes a happy-path test, but in production urgent jobs are late by up to 30 seconds, and throughput with 8 workers is the same as with 1.

Languages: Java · Kotlin
void submit(Job j) { synchronized (lock) { queue.add(j); } }

private void loop() {
    while (true) {
        synchronized (lock) {
            Job head = queue.peek();
            if (head == null) { lock.wait(); continue; }
            long wait = head.runAt - System.currentTimeMillis();
            if (wait > 0) { lock.wait(wait); }
            Job j = queue.poll();
            j.work.run();                         // run the job
        }
    }
}
fun submit(j: Job) = synchronized(lock) { queue.add(j) }

private fun loop() {
    while (true) {
        synchronized(lock) {
            val head = queue.peek()
            if (head == null) { lock.wait(); return@synchronized }
            val wait = head.runAt - System.currentTimeMillis()
            if (wait > 0) lock.wait(wait)
            queue.poll().work()                   // run the job
        }
    }
}
questions.promptHtml: Find all the defects and fix them.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: Notices only the missing notifyAll.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Are job durations long? Is shutdown required? Is a job allowed to throw?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Add notifyAll in submit, run jobs outside the lock.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) submit does not notify: a worker sleeping on a far head misses an earlier job (the 30 s lateness); (b) the job runs inside synchronized, so 8 workers serialise (throughput = 1 worker); (c) after wait(wait) returns the code polls without re-checking, so after an early wake-up it may run a job that is not due, or poll the wrong job if the head changed; (d) no exception handling, a throwing job kills the thread; (e) InterruptedException is not handled.
  4. How I'd verify each: Submit job due in 10 s then one due in 100 ms; assert the second runs at about 100 ms. Run 8 jobs of 200 ms on 8 workers; elapsed should be about 200 ms, not 1.6 s.
  5. Root cause: The critical section covers more than the queue manipulation and the wake-up protocol is incomplete.
  6. Fix: Re-check in a while, poll only when due, leave the monitor before running, catch per job, notify on submit (see the notes' loop).
Languages: Java · Kotlin
void submit(Job j) { synchronized (lock) { queue.add(j); lock.notifyAll(); } }
// loop: while(true){ synchronized(lock){ while(true){ ... if (wait <= 0) { j = queue.poll(); break; } lock.wait(wait);} }
//        try { j.work.run(); } catch (RuntimeException e) { log } }
fun submit(j: Job) = synchronized(lock) { queue.add(j); lock.notifyAll() }
// next(): while (!stopped) { head = peek(); if due -> poll; else lock.wait(wait) }  then run OUTSIDE the lock
  1. Prevention: Tests for earlier-job-while-sleeping and parallel execution; review checklist "no user code inside a lock".
  2. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I would not switch to notify(); notifyAll costs a few extra wake-ups but avoids a missed wake-up.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Could a spurious wakeup run a job early? -> Yes in this code; the while re-check fixes it.
  • How does DelayQueue avoid herd wake-ups? -> Leader/follower: only the leader does timed wait.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A background job runner held its lock while calling HTTP; one slow call froze every other tenant's jobs.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: finds one bug.
  • Hire: notify, run outside lock, re-check loop.
  • Strong hire: also exceptions, interrupts, and the tests that expose each defect.

questions.contextHtml: Product wants: (1) a failed job retries up to 5 times with exponential backoff (base 2 s); (2) recurring jobs every N seconds; (3) cancel a scheduled job by id. A developer implements retry as Thread.sleep(backoff); run() inside the worker, and cancel as queue.remove(job).
questions.promptHtml: What is wrong with that approach and how should each feature be added?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: Accepts the sleeping worker ("it works") and adds more worker threads.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Backoff jitter? Cap on delay? Are recurring jobs fixed-rate or fixed-delay? Should cancel stop a currently running job?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Remove the in-worker sleep.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) sleeping blocks one worker for the backoff time (with 8 workers and 8 retrying jobs all workers idle while due jobs wait); (b) queue.remove(obj) is O(n) and needs the lock; (c) recurring jobs implemented as loops hold a worker forever.
  4. How I'd verify each: Test: 8 failing jobs plus a due job; the due job must still run on time.
  5. Root cause: The scheduler already has the right primitive: re-submission with a new runAt.
  6. Fix: On failure, create the next attempt as a new Job with runAt = now + base * 2^n (plus jitter, capped) and attempt+1. Recurring: after the run, resubmit with runAt + period (fixed-rate) or now + period (fixed-delay). Cancel: volatile boolean cancelled on the job, checked when it is polled and again before running; the entry is dropped lazily.
Languages: Java · Kotlin
catch (RuntimeException e) {
    if (job.attempt < 5) submit(job.retry(now + (2000L << job.attempt)));
}
catch (e: RuntimeException) {
    if (job.attempt < 5) submit(job.retry(now + (2000L shl job.attempt)))
}
  1. Prevention: Tests for the backoff sequence (2, 4, 8, 16, 32 s) with an injected clock; cap and jitter to avoid retry storms.
  2. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Lazy cancel leaves dead entries in the heap until due; fine unless millions of cancellations (then compact). I would not retry forever; after 5 failures route to a dead-letter list.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• A thundering herd of retries after an outage? -> Add random jitter to each delay.
  • Cancelling a running job? -> Needs cooperative interruption via the job's own check.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: Retries without jitter after a database outage re-fired all failed jobs at the same second and took the database down again.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: sleeping in workers.
  • Hire: resubmit with new runAt, lazy cancel.
  • Strong hire: jitter, cap, dead-letter, fixed-rate vs fixed-delay.

questions.contextHtml: The scheduler test suite asserts Thread.sleep(150); assertEquals(1, ran.get()) and similar timings. On the shared CI box it fails about 1 run in 8, and the whole suite takes 40 s.
questions.promptHtml: How do you make the tests deterministic and fast, and what do you actually assert?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: Increases the sleeps to 500 ms.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Can the scheduler take a clock? Do tests need real wall time at all?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Replace sleeps with latches and short timeouts to unblock CI.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: CI jitter (GC, noisy neighbours) breaks exact-timing asserts; sleeps make the suite slow and still racy.
  4. How I'd verify each: Run the test 200 times in a loop; watch failure rate.
  5. Root cause: Tests assert elapsed milliseconds, which the scheduler never promises. The promise is order and exactly-once.
  6. Fix: Assert order and counts: a CountDownLatch released by each job, then compare the recorded order list. Use delays of tens of ms with wide gaps (100 ms apart). Inject a Clock/time source so ordering tests schedule at logical times and an advance method wakes workers.
Languages: Java · Kotlin
CountDownLatch done = new CountDownLatch(3);
List<String> order = Collections.synchronizedList(new ArrayList<>());
// submit jobs due at +100, +200, +300 in shuffled order
if (!done.await(2, TimeUnit.SECONDS)) fail();
assertEquals(List.of("soon", "mid", "late"), order);
val done = CountDownLatch(3)
val order = Collections.synchronizedList(mutableListOf<String>())
// submit jobs due at +100, +200, +300 in shuffled order
check(done.await(2, TimeUnit.SECONDS))
check(order == listOf("soon", "mid", "late"))
  1. Prevention: Test list: equal times resolved by priority, job submitted while workers sleep runs on time, throwing job leaves the worker alive, shutdown while idle returns, 10 producers submit 1,000 jobs each and all run exactly once.
  2. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I would not assert "ran within 5 ms". One or two coarse timing tests with generous bounds are fine.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Test the throwing job? -> Submit a throwing job, then a normal one; the normal one must still run.
  • Test shutdown semantics? -> Queue 100 future jobs, shutdown, assert none ran and join returned.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A 40 s timing suite was replaced by a latch-based one of 1.5 s; flake rate went from 12% to zero.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: longer sleeps.
  • Hire: latches, order assertions.
  • Strong hire: clock injection, producer stress test, explicit semantics tests.

questions.contextHtml:
A job service has 8 workers. Over a week the queue depth climbs from 0 to 90,000, but CPU is 5% and the process is up. jstack shows only 3 worker threads left; the other 5 are gone. Logs contain:

Exception in thread "w4" java.lang.NoClassDefFoundError: com/acme/PdfLib
    at ReportJob.run(ReportJob.java:44)
    at Scheduler.loop(Scheduler.java:127)

The loop catches RuntimeException only. A red herring: GC is healthy.
questions.promptHtml: Explain the failure, restore service, and fix the design.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Restart the service and add more threads."

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Are jobs idempotent (safe to rerun)? Why did a class go missing (bad deploy, classloader)? Is queued work durable?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Restart workers (rolling restart), keep the backlog if it is persisted; otherwise drain by priority.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) Error subclasses escape catch (RuntimeException) and terminate the worker thread, pool silently shrinks; (b) no supervision, so nothing notices; (c) the broken job is retried by hand and kills another worker.
  4. How I'd verify each: Count live worker threads (jstack | grep "w"), grep logs for Exception in thread "w; a unit test with a job throwing AssertionError.
  5. Root cause: The worker loop's safety net is narrower than the failures it can meet. A thread dies on the first uncaught throwable, and nobody replaces it.
  6. Fix: Catch Throwable around the job (rethrow only truly fatal VM errors after logging), keep the worker alive, and restore interrupt status. Add a metric for worker liveness and a supervisor that replaces dead workers, or use an ExecutorService which handles this for you.
Languages: Java · Kotlin
try { job.work.run(); }
catch (Throwable t) { log.error("job " + job.id + " failed", t); }   // worker survives
try { job.work() } catch (t: Throwable) { log.error("job ${job.id} failed", t) }
  1. Prevention: Gauges for live workers, queue depth and oldest job age; alert when workers < configured; an uncaught-exception handler that logs and respawns.
  2. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Catching Throwable can mask OutOfMemoryError; for fatal errors log loudly and let the supervisor decide to exit so the orchestrator restarts the pod.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Poison job that always kills? -> Cap attempts and move it to a dead-letter list.
  • Why not just use ThreadPoolExecutor? -> It replaces dead workers; for production I would.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A silent worker leak ran for days: dashboards showed healthy CPU because dead threads consume nothing.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: restart only.
  • Hire: catches Throwable, adds liveness metric.
  • Strong hire: supervisor, dead-letter, severity policy for fatal errors.

questions.contextHtml: The scheduler holds 5M pending jobs (session expiries, reminders) with 20,000 submissions/s and 12 workers. Symptoms: submit p99 600 ms, heap of 7 GB with 40% of time in GC, single lock contention shown in a profiler (all threads blocked on lock). Also the JVM restart loses everything.
questions.promptHtml: What changes do you make to the data structure, locking and durability, and in what order?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Add more workers" or "move to Kafka" without reasoning.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Required precision (1 ms or 1 s)? Are most timers cancelled before firing? Must jobs survive restart? Is the work itself fast?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Reduce memory per job (drop payload objects, store ids), shorten the critical section.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) one lock for 20,000 submits/s plus peeks serialises everything; (b) a 5M-node heap of objects creates GC pressure; (c) heap insert O(log 5M) is about 22 comparisons, not the main issue; (d) durability is a separate requirement.
  4. How I'd verify each: Lock contention profile, GC logs, allocation profile per job.
  5. Root cause: A single global structure with a single lock was designed for thousands of jobs, not millions.
  6. Fix: Short term: shard into K queues by job id hash, each with its own lock and a small number of workers (or one timer thread per shard). Medium: a hierarchical timing wheel at 1 s resolution (O(1) insert, buckets store compact job ids). Durable: persist in a database or Redis and have workers claim due rows:
SELECT id FROM jobs WHERE run_at <= now() ORDER BY run_at LIMIT 100
FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED;
  1. Prevention: Soak test at 2x expected volume; metrics for lock wait, queue depth per shard, lateness (actual minus intended run time).
  2. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: A wheel gives up precision for speed; fine for expiries, not for sub-millisecond scheduling. Sharding loses global priority order: higher-priority jobs are only ordered within a shard, which I would state.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• One shard gets a hot key? -> Hash by job id, not tenant, unless fairness per tenant is needed.
  • Why SKIP LOCKED? -> Workers skip rows locked by others instead of waiting, so many workers share the queue without blocking.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A reminder system moved from a global heap to hashed wheel buckets and cut submit p99 from seconds to a few milliseconds.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: more threads or a buzzword.
  • Hire: sharding or wheel plus DB claim query.
  • Strong hire: quantifies the problem, names the precision and ordering trade-offs, sequences changes.

questions.contextHtml: The spec says only: "The scheduler must shut down gracefully." During a rolling deploy, 3,000 queued jobs are lost, 12 running jobs are cut in half, and one worker hangs forever because a job is blocked on a socket. Different stakeholders say: billing wants no lost jobs, ops wants the pod gone within 30 seconds.
questions.promptHtml: Pin down what graceful means and implement it.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: System.exit after shutdown, or join() with no timeout.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Are jobs idempotent? Are queued jobs durable? What is the pod termination grace period? Which jobs may be dropped?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Stop accepting new jobs first; give running jobs a deadline.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: Options: (a) drop queued, finish running; (b) drain everything (may exceed 30 s); (c) persist the queue and exit fast; running jobs get a bounded wait then interrupt.
  4. How I'd verify each: Test: submit 1,000 jobs, call shutdown, count completed, dropped, interrupted.
  5. Root cause: "Graceful" was never defined, so each implementation chose silently.
  6. Fix: Define states RUNNING -> DRAINING -> STOPPED. shutdown(): reject new submits, set flag, notifyAll. Workers finish the current job and exit when the flag is set. awaitTermination(30 s): after the deadline interrupt workers; jobs must honour interruption. Queued but not started jobs are either persisted (preferred for billing) or returned to the caller as a list (as ExecutorService.shutdownNow does).
Languages: Java · Kotlin
List<Job> shutdownNow() {
    synchronized (lock) { stopped = true; lock.notifyAll(); }
    for (Thread t : workers) t.interrupt();
    synchronized (lock) { return new ArrayList<>(queue); }   // caller persists them
}
fun shutdownNow(): List<Job> {
    synchronized(lock) { stopped = true; lock.notifyAll() }
    threads.forEach { it.interrupt() }
    return synchronized(lock) { queue.toList() }
}
  1. Prevention: Idempotent jobs and a persisted queue; test that shutdown with a hung job still returns within the deadline.
  2. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I would not wait forever (join() with no timeout); I would not silently drop queued jobs without returning or persisting them.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Job ignores interrupts (blocked on socket read)? -> Use socket timeouts, or close the resource; last resort is process exit and a durable queue so the job reruns.
  • Submit during shutdown? -> Throw RejectedExecution-style error so callers know.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A deploy script killed pods with 30 s grace while jobs ran for 5 minutes; every deploy silently dropped hundreds of exports.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: exit or unbounded join.
  • Hire: states, stop accepting, deadline plus interrupt.
  • Strong hire: separates drain vs drop, returns or persists leftover jobs, ties to platform grace period.
